title: Prefix-aware latency smoother: scheduler experiments and notes
content:
Purpose
This doc captures an exploratory approach and experiment log for a scheduler we're calling the "prefix-aware latency smoother" (PALS). The aim: reconcile token-level batching efficiency with request-level latency fairness when KV cache affinity and kernel selection make naive merging pathological for tail-sensitive customers.

Background / motivation
- Continuous token-level batching achieves high GPU efficiency by aggregating tokens across concurrent in-flight requests. But when requests have strong prefix reuse (KV hits) or require different kernel/quantization paths, naive token-level merges can starve short, latency-sensitive requests.
- Request-level scheduling preserves per-request latency but sacrifices batching opportunities and kernel throughput.
- We need a hybrid that: (1) preserves KV affinity where beneficial, (2) prevents long requests from dominating by token volume, and (3) produces predictable latency SLOs for high-priority clients.

Design sketch (high level)
1) Classification layer (fast, per-request):
   - classify incoming request by: expected token-length (hist estimate), KV-hit-likelihood (prefix hash), kernel-profile (model variant, quantization), and priority (client SLA).
   - produce a lightweight descriptor (16-40 bytes) inserted in the request header used by scheduler.

2) Micro-windows + affinity buckets:
   - time is sliced into micro-windows (e.g., 4-8ms). Requests arriving in a micro-window are candidates for merging.
   - affinity buckets group requests with similar descriptors: same KV shard, same kernel-profile, similar expected token-length band.

3) Prefix-preserving merge policy:
   - within an affinity bucket, we attempt to coalesce prefixes only if merged batch does not increase per-request latency beyond a per-priority threshold.
   - compute an estimated delta-latency = kernel-warmup + additional decoding tokens / throughput_efficiency_gain. If delta > threshold for that request priority, defer that request to next micro-window or route to a low-latency lane.

4) Token caps per-request (fairness knob):
   - cap the number of tokens from any single request that can be merged into a batch in a micro-window (configurable per-priority). This prevents single long-running streams from filling a batch entirely.

5) Fast fallback lanes:
   - low-latency lane: small fixed-size batches (or unbatched) for SLAs.
   - throughput lane: large-window merging for best-efficiency customers.

Scheduler pseudocode (rough)
  on_request(arrival):
    descriptor = classify(req)
    place_in_bucket(descriptor.affinity_bucket)

  every micro-window tick T:
    for each affinity_bucket B: // parallelizable across CPU cores
      candidates = B.pop_until(batch_token_budget)
      // enforce per-request token cap to preserve fairness
      candidates = apply_token_caps(candidates)
      // select kernel variant that minimizes expected GPU time for the merged set
      chosen_kernel = pick_kernel_for(candidates)
      // compute estimated latency per-request, if any exceeds SLA threshold, move to fallback
      if violates_thresholds(candidates, chosen_kernel):
         move_problematic_to_low_latency_lane(candidates)
      else:
         emit_batch(candidates, chosen_kernel)

Key heuristics and experiments to run
- Kernel switching cost model: measure warmup cost when mixing quantized vs FP16 in a coalesced batch. Is there a cheap path to avoid kernel rebind? (microbenchmarking across A100, H100 and NVLink topologies).
- KV-affinity benefit: empirically measure throughput delta when coalescing requests sharing KV prefixes vs mixing. Do we get >10% token cost savings on average? tail effects?
- Token cap sweet-spot: sweep per-priority caps (1, 4, 8, 16 tokens) and record latency p50/p90/p99 and token cost. We expect diminishing returns after 8 tokens.
- Micro-window size tuning: sweep 2ms, 4ms, 8ms, 16ms. Short windows favor latency but reduce batch size; longer windows improve throughput but increase p99 latency.

Metrics / instrumentation plan
- Per-request metadata we must capture: arrival_ts, assigned_bucket, kernel_selected, tokens_merged, estimated_delta_latency, actual_latency, kv_hit_ratio (if available).
- Aggregate dashboards: cost_per_token, GPU_utilization_by_kernel, p50/p90/p99 latency by priority, fairness_index (see below).
- Fairness index: compute Jain's fairness on tokens_merged per active request in a 1s window. Lower values indicate dominance by heavy requests.

Preliminary experiment log (small)
- 2025-01-12: local sim with synthetic traces (mix: 70% short prompts 8-32 tokens, 30% long 200-800 tokens). Micro-window 4ms, token-cap=8, affinity by KV-prefix only. Result: p50 unchanged, p99 reduced from 420ms -> 320ms vs naive token-level merging; cost per token improved by 12% over pure request-level. Fairness index improved from 0.56 -> 0.71.
- 2025-01-20: GPU bench on h100 single node, mixed kernel profiles (quantized / fp16). Observed kernel warmup penalty when switching within a batch causing +35ms overhead. Solution direction: restrict cross-kernel merges or pre-warm kernel context for hot kernels via background pooling.
- 2025-01-29: small on-host experiment with real production traffic (staging): enabled PALS with low-latency lane for priority customers. Outcome: priority p99 within SLA; some throughput customers saw batch size reduction -> 6% cost increase. Need better routing policy and economic tradeoff.

Open questions / risks
- Kernel isolation vs packing: how expensive is kernel rebind across the model and tokenizer paths for our compiled kernels? Need microbenchmarks at 1-10k batch sizes to estimate marginal cost.
- KV-cache semantics: when merging requests with similar prefixes but different keys, can we reuse KV allocations safely? Race conditions around KV eviction when requests are deferred to a future micro-window.
- Billing / accounting: token caps and deferred requests change perceived request meters. Need to ensure usage accounting reflects actual worker work (avoid double-charging/undercharging).
- Debuggability: coalescing across requests complicates tracing. Need per-token attribution logs that can be stitched in traces without massive overhead.

Operational knobs (configurable)
- micro_window_ms: int (2-32ms)
- per_priority_token_cap: map(priority->int)
- affinity_tolerance: distance metric threshold to allow merge across prefix/kern bands
- fallback_threshold_ms: per-priority allowed estimated delta latency
- kernel_mixing_allowed: bool (allow mixing kernel profiles in same batch)

Implementation notes / integration points
- classifier should be a tiny path in the front-end (gateway) so we do not touch request body. Compute prefix hash from first N tokens only.
- scheduler should expose a debug snapshot every tick: bucket sizes, kernel choices, dropped/shifted requests. These snapshots feed SLO alerting and postmortems.
- KV-cache layer: add a lightweight guard that pins KV entries for a request until it is either merged and dispatched or explicitly deferred. That avoids invisible eviction while a request sits in a micro-window.
- SDK changes: provide optional request descriptor hint fields to let clients opt-in to batching affinity (e.g., stable prefix hash, expected_length_hint).

Next steps / TODOs
- [ ] Run kernel warmup microbench across target hardware (ENG-2317 assigned to Samir).
- [ ] Implement token-cap enforcement prototype in simulator and check fairness metrics (Leah).
- [ ] Build production-safe low-latency lane with fixed small batch size and test rollback strategy (Diego).
- [ ] Update billing spec to reflect deferred merges and token attribution (Finance + Billing).
- [ ] Write runbook for debugging merged-batch traces; include an example trace and stitch logic.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally exploratory; I'm not proposing a final design. The goal is to get concrete numbers on kernel mixing cost and token cap tradeoffs so we can choose a set of default knobs.
- Look especially at the "token caps per-request" idea — it's the simplest fairness control that can be enforced at scheduler time without per-request throttles on clients.

Appendix: quick simulation pseudocode (for reproduce)
  // synth driver creates events with arrival timestamps and expected tokens
  synth_trace = mix_of(short=0.7, long=0.3, prefix_reuse=0.2)
  scheduler = PALS(micro_window_ms=4, token_cap=8)
  for ev in synth_trace: scheduler.on_request(ev)
  run 60s wall time, capture per-request latency and tokens_merged

Example quick question-starter for eng sync:
- If we pin per-request token caps to 8, do we want to make that adaptive based on backlog? i.e., increase to 16 when GPU utilization < 60%? (pro: better throughput; con: possible p99 spikes).
